issue.mint_text: Mexico City (Mo, below the radiant cap on the reverse)

new.story: One of Mexico's best-loved coin designs, struck in bronze from 1943: the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan fills the reverse, its name carved at the pyramid's base, with the twin volcanoes Iztaccihuatl and Popocatepetl smoking behind it and a radiant Liberty cap dividing the big 20 overhead. Mexico authorized the type in August 1943, in the middle of the Second World War, to replace the silver twenty centavos it could no longer afford to strike - this is a first-year piece, one of some 46 million poured out that year. The obverse carries the national arms, the eagle on its cactus with the snake, and the words ESTADOS UNIDOS MEXICANOS.
new.notes: Both sides photographed in the holder. Transcription from the coin: ESTADOS UNIDOS MEXICANOS around the national arms; reverse 20 divided by the radiant cap, Mo below it, the Teotihuacan pyramid scene, CENTAVOS in a plaque, date below. The date was read digit-by-digit from contrast-enhanced crops as 1-9-4-3; the final digit is worn and at full-frame distance first suggested 1942, but 1942 is impossible for this coin - the bronze pyramid type began in 1943, and a 1942 twenty centavos would be the small silver issue - so the reading stands as 1943. The coin is dark-toned bronze with honest circulation wear.

source: photo NOID_Mexico_1943_20Centavos_obv.jpeg (pen label: MEXICO 1943 20 CENTAVOS); date verified from enhanced crops and the type's 1943 start year, 2026-11-09
